EQUIPMENT LEASE AGREEMENT
Between Titanpoint Leasing Corp. ("Lessor") and Solmere Energy, Inc. ("Lessee")
Equipment: Solar panel maintenance robotic arm units (4 units, Model RX-4) | Effective Date: April 1

RECITALS
Lessor leases specialized maintenance equipment to Lessee for use at Lessee's solar field sites. An earlier quote provided to Lessee on February 10 proposed a flat $10,000 early termination fee regardless of remaining term. That quote was not adopted; the final terms below use a different formula, described in Section 2.

1. TERM AND PAYMENTS
This lease runs 48 months from the Effective Date. Lessee pays $3,200 per month, due on the 1st of each month, by ACH transfer to Lessor's designated account.

2. EARLY TERMINATION
If Lessee terminates this lease before the end of the 48-month term for any reason other than Lessor's uncured material breach, Lessee shall pay an early termination fee equal to the GREATER of (a) $15,000, or (b) 25% of the total remaining monthly payments that would have been due through the end of the original term. This fee is due within 15 days of the termination date.

3. MAINTENANCE AND RISK OF LOSS
Lessee is responsible for routine maintenance per the manufacturer's schedule, including quarterly calibration by a certified technician. Risk of loss passes to Lessee upon delivery and remains with Lessee throughout the term regardless of where the equipment is deployed among Lessee's various solar field sites.

4. COMPARISON NOTE
For internal reference, Lessee separately leases delivery trucks from a different lessor, Fenwick Fleet Leasing, under an unrelated agreement with a flat $8,000 early termination fee regardless of remaining term. That truck lease is entirely separate from this Agreement, covers different equipment, and its flat-fee structure does not apply here.

5. INSURANCE
Lessee shall maintain comprehensive insurance on the equipment naming Lessor as loss payee, with coverage of at least the equipment's full replacement value throughout the term, and shall provide proof of coverage annually.

6. RETURN CONDITION
Upon expiration or termination, Lessee returns all units in good working condition, ordinary wear excepted. Lessor may charge repair costs against Lessee's security deposit of $5,000 held since the Effective Date, with any shortfall billed separately.

7. DEFAULT
Failure to pay any amount within 10 days of its due date is a default. Lessor may repossess equipment after 30 days of continuing default, in addition to any other remedy, including the early termination fee under Section 2 if Lessor elects to treat the default as an early termination rather than pursuing the unpaid amounts directly.

8. GENERAL
This Agreement is the entire agreement between the parties regarding the leased equipment and supersedes the February 10 quote and any other prior proposal or discussion.

CURRENT STATUS NOTE (added by Lessee's finance team, October 12)
As of this month, 20 monthly payments remain on the original 48-month term (28 have been made). Lessee's operations team has informally asked finance to model the cost of terminating early to switch to owned equipment instead of leasing. Finance calculated the remaining payments at 20 x $3,200 = $64,000, meaning 25% of remaining payments would be $16,000, which is higher than the $15,000 flat floor, so the fee under Section 2(b) would govern if termination happened today. No decision to terminate has actually been made; this note is for internal planning purposes only and has not been shared with Lessor.

SIGNATURES
For Titanpoint Leasing Corp.: Rafael Obi, Contracts Manager
For Solmere Energy, Inc.: Marisol Vega, VP Operations

EXHIBIT A — EQUIPMENT SCHEDULE
Four RX-4 robotic arm units, serial numbers RX4-0117 through RX4-0120, each delivered April 1 to Lessee's central staging yard before onward deployment to individual solar field sites as needed.

AMBERFIELD UNIFIED SCHOOL DISTRICT
Board of Education Meeting Minutes
Date: May 8 | Recorded by: Ingrid Halvorsen, Board Clerk

ATTENDANCE
Present: President Tariq Idris, Vice President Beatrice Adeyemi, Members Gideon Farley, Consuela Marques, Wanjiru Kamau. Superintendent Amara Chukwu also present.

CALL TO ORDER
President Idris called the meeting to order at 6:00 p.m. and reviewed tonight's two main agenda items: transportation route changes and a proposed teacher stipend program, noting both had generated significant community interest ahead of tonight's meeting.

TRANSPORTATION: ROUTE CONSOLIDATION
Superintendent Chukwu presented a transportation efficiency study recommending three changes: merging Route 12 and Route 15 into a single route, since both currently run under 60% capacity and serve overlapping neighborhoods; eliminating Route 9 entirely and reassigning its 22 students to Route 7; and adding one new route, Route 18, to serve a newly opened subdivision. After parent comments raising concern that Route 9's elimination would add 25 minutes to some students' commute, the board considered the three items separately rather than as a single package. Consuela Marques moved to approve merging Routes 12 and 15, projected to save $85,000 annually. The motion passed 5-0. Gideon Farley then moved to approve eliminating Route 9. After further discussion, this motion failed 2-3, with Farley and Marques in favor and Idris, Adeyemi, and Kamau opposed, citing the commute-time concern raised by parents. Route 9 continues to operate unchanged. Wanjiru Kamau then moved to approve adding new Route 18 to serve the subdivision, at an estimated cost of $62,000 annually. The motion passed 5-0.

TEACHER STIPEND PROGRAM
Beatrice Adeyemi presented a proposal to fund a $500 per-teacher stipend for teachers who lead after-school tutoring sessions at least twice a week, aimed at addressing pandemic-era learning gaps. District staff estimate 40 teachers district-wide would qualify this year, for a total program cost of $20,000, funded from a one-time state grant earmarked specifically for learning recovery. The board discussed whether to cap the number of participating teachers; Superintendent Chukwu recommended against a cap in the first year to encourage broad participation. Gideon Farley moved to approve the stipend program as presented, uncapped, for this school year only, to be reevaluated before any renewal. The motion passed 5-0.

BUDGET IMPACT DISCUSSION
The treasurer's office, represented by Wanjiru Kamau, noted the net transportation budget impact this year is an increase of about $62,000 in new costs from Route 18, partially offset by the $85,000 in savings from the Route 12/15 merger, for a net transportation savings of approximately $23,000 overall. This transportation figure is separate from and does not draw on the state learning-recovery grant funding the teacher stipend program described above.

PRIOR PROPOSAL REFERENCE
President Idris noted that a similar route-elimination proposal for Route 9 was also brought to the board two years ago and was likewise rejected at that time, for similar commute-time concerns raised by a different group of parents; tonight's vote is consistent with that prior decision rather than representing any new position from the board.

PUBLIC COMMENT
Four parents spoke during public comment: three expressed relief that Route 9 was preserved, and one asked when Route 18 would begin service. Superintendent Chukwu confirmed Route 18 is targeted to launch at the start of the fall semester, pending final approval of the bus vendor contract at a future meeting.

ADJOURNMENT
Meeting adjourned at 7:50 p.m. Next meeting: June 12.

Minutes submitted by Ingrid Halvorsen, Board Clerk.

ATTACHMENT NOTE
A copy of the full transportation efficiency study, including capacity figures for all district routes, is available on request from the Superintendent's office and will be posted to the district website within one week of this meeting for public reference.

KESTREL AEROSPACE PARTS — PAYROLL COMPLIANCE AUDIT
Subject: Overtime Calculation Review, Pay Periods March-April
Prepared by: Internal Audit (Lead: Piotr Zielinski)
Date Issued: May 15

SCOPE
This audit reviewed overtime pay calculations for all non-exempt hourly employees across six pay periods, March 1 through April 25, to confirm compliance with state law requiring overtime pay at 1.5 times the regular hourly rate for all hours worked over 40 in a single work week, calculated on a weekly basis regardless of the employer's pay period length.

METHODOLOGY
Auditors recalculated expected gross pay for every non-exempt employee in every sampled week from raw timeclock data and compared it to actual payroll disbursements, flagging any discrepancy over $10 for further review and root-cause analysis.

FINDING: DECLAN MORIARTY, WEEK OF MARCH 17
Timeclock data shows Declan Moriarty, a warehouse technician paid $24.00 per hour, worked 46 hours during the week of March 17: 40 regular hours and 6 overtime hours. Correct pay under the 1.5x overtime rule: 40 hours x $24.00 = $960.00 regular pay, plus 6 hours x $24.00 x 1.5 = $216.00 overtime pay, for a total of $1,176.00. Payroll records show Declan was actually paid $1,104.00 for that week, calculated as 46 hours x $24.00 flat with no overtime premium applied at all. This is an underpayment of $72.00, caused by a timesheet-import error that misclassified his hours as entirely regular time rather than splitting regular and overtime hours correctly.

FINDING: SELIN AYDIN, WEEK OF MARCH 17 (FOR COMPARISON)
In the same week, Selin Aydin, also a warehouse technician paid $24.00 per hour, worked 44 hours. Her pay was correctly calculated: 40 x $24.00 = $960.00 plus 4 x $24.00 x 1.5 = $144.00, totaling $1,104.00, correctly paid in full. Her case is included here only to confirm the payroll system's overtime formula itself works correctly when hours are classified properly; the March 17 issue was isolated to Declan's specific timesheet import, not a systemic formula error affecting the payroll system broadly.

SCOPE OF THE ERROR
Auditors traced the root cause to a one-time manual correction to Declan's timesheet on March 15, fixing an unrelated clock-in error from March 13, that inadvertently reset his hour-type classification for the entire week to "regular" before the payroll export ran. No other employee's records show the same manual-correction pattern in the six sampled pay periods, and no other discrepancies over the $10 threshold were found across the full sample of hourly employees reviewed.

REMEDIATION
Declan Moriarty was issued a retroactive payment of $72.00 on May 1, once the discrepancy was confirmed through this audit. Payroll has added a validation check that flags any timesheet where a manual correction touches hour-type classification, requiring a second reviewer's sign-off before export, specifically to catch this failure mode going forward before checks are issued.

POLICY PROPOSAL CONSIDERED
During the audit, a manager suggested calculating overtime on a bi-weekly averaged basis instead of weekly, which would have smoothed Declan's hours differently and arguably simplified payroll's timesheet-correction process going forward. Internal Audit and Legal reviewed this and rejected it outright, noting state law specifically requires weekly overtime calculation, and a bi-weekly averaging approach would be unlawful regardless of any administrative convenience, not merely a policy preference to weigh against cost.

CONCLUSION
This audit found one isolated, corrected underpayment, $72.00 for Declan Moriarty for the week of March 17, caused by a timesheet-import error, not a systemic overtime-formula problem. No other discrepancies were found across the six-pay-period sample.

This audit's findings and remediation status will be reported to the Finance Committee at its next scheduled meeting.

Signed, Piotr Zielinski, Lead Auditor, Internal Audit.

ALDERPOINT HEALTH — MEDICATION SAFETY NEAR-MISS REPORT
Unit: Cardiac Step-Down, 4th Floor | Report No. MED-0271
Event Date: October 6 | Report Date: October 13
Prepared by: Patient Safety Committee (Chair: Consuela Marques)

EVENT SUMMARY
On October 6 at approximately 3:40 p.m., Nurse Priyanka Chatterjee identified a dosage discrepancy before administering a scheduled medication to a patient. The electronic order specified 50 mg of the medication, but the attending physician's verbal order, given by phone at 2:15 p.m. and transcribed into the EHR by a covering resident, was actually for 5 mg. The order was transcribed with an extra zero, a tenfold overdose as entered into the system. Nurse Chatterjee, following standard practice of cross-checking any dose that seemed unusually high against the medication's typical range, flagged the order before administration. No dose was given at the incorrect amount; this event is classified as a near-miss with no patient harm.

VERIFICATION AND CORRECTION
Nurse Chatterjee paged the attending physician to confirm the intended dose, who confirmed 5 mg was correct. The order was corrected in the EHR at 3:52 p.m., and the correct 5 mg dose was administered at 4:05 p.m., within the medication's normal administration window for that patient.

ROOT CAUSE
The root cause is identified as a transcription error during a verbal order, compounded by the absence of a mandatory read-back step at the time the order was entered. The covering resident who transcribed the order stated in interview that they did not read the dose back to the attending physician for confirmation before entering it, which is not currently a mandatory step for verbal orders under existing policy, though it has long been considered a best practice by the committee.

DISTINCTION FROM PRIOR INCIDENT
This report should not be conflated with a separate incident last quarter, MED-0198, on a different unit, General Medicine, in which a similar tenfold transcription error was not caught before administration and did reach a patient, resulting in temporary but resolved adverse effects requiring overnight monitoring. That incident was already closed with its own corrective actions in August, before this October near-miss occurred. The present report is a new, independent event on a different unit, though it shares a similar failure mode, which the Patient Safety Committee views as relevant context suggesting the read-back gap identified in August's corrective actions may not yet be fully effective house-wide.

DISCUSSION OF RESPONSES
Some committee members proposed eliminating verbal orders entirely, requiring all orders to be entered directly into the EHR by the ordering physician in person or via a secure terminal. This was discussed and not adopted; the committee agreed this would be impractical during emergencies or when the ordering physician is not at a workstation, and could introduce its own dangerous delays in urgent situations. Instead, the committee is adopting a mandatory read-back requirement specifically for all verbal orders house-wide: the person receiving a verbal order must read the full order, including dose and units, back to the ordering physician and receive explicit verbal confirmation before entering it into the EHR.

ACTIONS ADOPTED
1. Mandatory read-back for all verbal orders, house-wide, effective November 1 (owner: Chief Medical Officer).
2. EHR system to add a soft alert flagging any entered dose more than 5 times the medication's standard reference dose, requiring a second click to confirm, by December 1 (owner: IT Clinical Systems).
3. Re-audit read-back compliance on General Medicine specifically, given MED-0198, within 30 days of the November 1 policy start (owner: Consuela Marques).

RECOGNITION
The committee formally recognizes Nurse Chatterjee's dose-range cross-check as the reason this event resulted in no patient harm, consistent with existing best practice even before today's policy change makes a related step mandatory for everyone.

SIGN-OFF
Approved by the Patient Safety Committee, October 13.

Project: Dashboard UI redesign | Effective Date: July 1

Contractor will design updated user-interface mockups and a component style guide for Client's dashboard product, per the scope in Exhibit A, targeted for completion within 8 weeks of the Effective Date, subject to timely feedback from Client at each review checkpoint.

BACKGROUND
The committee reviewed the independent reserve study completed by Meridian Reserve Advisors in March, covering a 30-year capital projection for roof, elevator, façade, and mechanical systems across the property's three towers. The study concluded that the current monthly reserve contribution of $45 per unit is significantly underfunded relative to projected future capital needs, and recommends increasing the contribution to $68 per unit per month, a 51% increase, phased in as the committee sees fit, in order to reach full funding over the full 30-year horizon.

DISCUSSION
Chair Uzo noted that jumping straight to $68 per unit in a single year would likely generate significant owner pushback and hardship for fixed-income owners on the property. Zara Whitmore proposed instead a one-time special assessment of $2,000 per unit to shore up the reserve immediately, combined with keeping the ongoing monthly contribution at $45. After discussion, the committee felt a special assessment would be harder for owners to budget for than a gradual monthly increase spread over time, and voted 3-1, Whitmore opposed, to recommend against the special-assessment approach in favor of a phased monthly increase instead.

RECOMMENDATION TO THE BOARD
The committee recommends the board approve raising the monthly reserve contribution to $55 per unit effective July 1 this year, as the first step of a three-year phase-in toward the study's recommended $68 per unit, with the second and third steps to be set at each of the next two annual budget meetings based on updated reserve balances and any material change in projected capital costs. Colin Draper moved to adopt this phased recommendation; Rosalind Kanu seconded. The motion passed 4-0, with Whitmore's earlier special-assessment proposal already having been voted down, since she supported the phased alternative as the next-best option once her own preferred approach failed.

BOARD LIAISON REPORT
Gideon Farley confirmed the full board will vote on the committee's $55-per-unit recommendation at its May 10 meeting, and noted the board is not obligated to adopt the committee's recommendation exactly as written, though the board has generally followed reserve committee recommendations closely in past years.

FINANCIAL CONTEXT
Rosalind Kanu presented the current reserve fund balance: $410,000 across 180 units. At the current $45 per unit contribution, the fund grows by about $97,200 per year before any capital expenditures are subtracted; the study projects this pace is insufficient to cover a roof replacement projected at $1.8 million in year 12 and elevator modernization projected at $2.4 million in year 18, among other planned expenditures across the 30-year horizon.

NEXT STEPS
The committee will prepare an owner-facing summary of the reserve study findings and the phased-increase rationale for distribution before the May 10 board meeting, so owners understand the recommendation before the board votes on it. Emeka Uzo will draft this summary by April 29 for full committee review and comment before it goes out.

ADJOURNMENT
Meeting adjourned at 8:10 p.m. with no further business raised.

Minutes respectfully submitted by Lucia Ferraro.

APPENDIX: OWNER QUESTIONS FIELDED AFTER THE MEETING
Two owners approached Chair Uzo informally after adjournment asking whether the phased increase could be revisited downward if actual roof and elevator costs come in below the study's projections when those projects are eventually bid out. Uzo noted the committee's recommendation is based on the reserve study's current projections, and confirmed the board can adjust future phase-in steps at each annual budget meeting if updated bids or reserve balances warrant a smaller increase than originally planned.

COBALT PEAK SOFTWARE — THIRD-PARTY VENDOR RISK ASSESSMENT
Prepared by: Vendor Risk Management (Lead: Samir Kassab)
Date Issued: September 5
Scope: Annual risk-tier review of vendors with access to customer or company data

METHODOLOGY
Each vendor is scored against three factors: certification status (SOC2 Type II or equivalent), scope of data access (PII, aggregate/anonymized, or none), and incident history in the past 24 months. Vendors are placed in High, Medium, or Low risk tiers based on a weighted combination of these three factors per the Vendor Risk Policy VR-3, reviewed annually for every vendor with any form of data access to company or customer systems.

FINDINGS: DATAFLOW ANALYTICS
DataFlow Analytics provides customer analytics processing and has access to customer PII, including names and email addresses, for its core service. DataFlow does not currently hold a SOC2 Type II certification; it holds only a self-attested security questionnaire response, last updated 18 months ago and never independently verified. Combined with PII access and no recent independent certification, DataFlow is rated HIGH RISK this year.

FINDINGS: CLOUDMAILER
CloudMailer provides transactional email delivery and has broad access to customer email addresses and message content, but holds a current SOC2 Type II certification renewed four months ago, with no security incidents in the past 24 months. Despite the broad data access, the current certification and clean incident history place CloudMailer in the MEDIUM RISK tier this year.

FINDINGS: SNAPINVOICE
SnapInvoice provides invoice-generation services with access limited to aggregate billing totals only, no PII fields whatsoever, and holds a current SOC2 Type II certification of its own. SnapInvoice is rated LOW RISK this year.

FINDINGS: PIXELFRAME (FOR CONTEXT, PRIOR YEAR)
Last year's assessment rated a different vendor, PixelFrame, a former image-hosting vendor, as High Risk for reasons similar to DataFlow's current rating. PixelFrame's contract was not renewed this year for unrelated business reasons, since the internal team migrated to a different in-house solution, so PixelFrame is not part of this year's active vendor list and is mentioned only because a board member asked about it during the review meeting.

DISCUSSION OF RESPONSE OPTIONS
One proposal discussed was to immediately terminate all vendor relationships rated High Risk, effective immediately, to eliminate exposure as fast as possible. This was not adopted; Vendor Risk Management and Legal noted DataFlow's service is difficult to replace on short notice and immediate termination could disrupt core analytics functions without any transition plan in place. Instead, the adopted policy gives DataFlow a 90-day remediation window to obtain SOC2 Type II certification or provide a credible certification timeline; if that window passes without adequate progress, the contract will be terminated at that point rather than being terminated immediately today.

REMEDIATION TRACKING
DataFlow has been notified of the 90-day window, beginning September 5 and running through December 4. A check-in review is scheduled for October 20 to assess progress toward certification and decide whether the timeline still looks credible.

RECOMMENDATIONS
1. DataFlow Analytics: enforce the 90-day remediation window; prepare a transition plan in parallel in case certification is not achieved by December 4.
2. CloudMailer: no immediate action; re-assess at next annual review given the broad data access despite current good standing.
3. SnapInvoice: no action needed; continue on the standard annual review cycle going forward.

FOLLOW-UP SCHEDULE
In addition to the October 20 DataFlow check-in, Vendor Risk Management will present a full status update on all three active vendors at the December board meeting, incorporating any changes to DataFlow's certification progress and confirming whether CloudMailer's and SnapInvoice's ratings remain accurate given any changes to their own data-access scope during the year.

SIGN-OFF
Reviewed and accepted by Samir Kassab, Vendor Risk Lead, and the CISO, September 5.

VANTAGE ANALYTICS — DATA CENTER INCIDENT REPORT
Facility: Meridian Colocation Site, Pod 3 | Report No. DC-INC-0089
Incident Date: January 18 | Report Date: January 24
Prepared by: Infrastructure Operations (Lead: Bram Vandermeer)

SUMMARY
On January 18 at 2:10 a.m., a cooling unit failure in Pod 3 caused ambient temperature to rise steadily from a normal baseline of 68°F. The failure was caused by a failed compressor in Cooling Unit 3-B, one of two redundant units serving Pod 3; Cooling Unit 3-A remained fully operational throughout but could not fully compensate for 3-B's failure under that night's server load.

TIMELINE
02:10 - Cooling Unit 3-B fails; temperature begins rising steadily.
02:25 - Temperature reaches 80°F; monitoring dashboard shows an elevated-temperature warning, visible to the on-call engineer but not yet paging anyone.
02:40 - Temperature reaches 85°F; automated warning escalates to a page. On-call engineer Keiko Sano acknowledges within 4 minutes of the page.
02:55 - Temperature reaches 90°F, triggering the automated non-critical-server shutdown policy: all servers tagged "non-critical" in Pod 3 power down automatically to reduce heat load, per existing runbook policy.
03:05 - Temperature peaks at 95°F before beginning to decline as the shutdown reduces heat load and Cooling Unit 3-A continues operating at full capacity.
03:40 - Facilities technician arrives on-site and begins repair on Cooling Unit 3-B.
05:15 - Cooling Unit 3-B repaired and back online; temperature returns to 68°F baseline by 05:45.
06:00 - Non-critical servers powered back on in a staggered sequence to avoid a new load spike; all restored by 06:40.

IMPACT
No hardware damage was recorded; server internal temperature logs confirm no individual unit exceeded its rated maximum operating temperature, since the room-level 95°F peak stayed well under the equipment's own tolerance even before the automated shutdown reduced heat generation further. Non-critical services were unavailable from 02:55 to 06:40, approximately 3 hours 45 minutes total. Critical, customer-facing services, which are on a separate policy and were not shut down, saw no interruption at all; critical-tier hardware is rated for higher ambient tolerance specifically to remain online during exactly this kind of event.

DISTINCT FROM POD 1 EVENT
Separately, on January 20, Pod 1 experienced a brief power blip lasting under one second, causing a handful of non-redundant lab servers to restart on their own. This was traced to an unrelated utility-side voltage sag and required no incident response beyond automatic restart of the affected machines. Pod 1's event is unrelated to Pod 3's cooling failure, involves entirely different equipment and a different root cause, and caused no service impact beyond the lab servers restarting.

ROOT CAUSE
Cooling Unit 3-B's compressor failed due to a worn bearing that had shown early warning vibration signs in a routine inspection two months earlier, but was scheduled for replacement during a maintenance window that had not yet occurred. That maintenance had been scheduled for February, five weeks after this failure actually happened.

DISCUSSION OF RESPONSES
One engineer proposed lowering the automated non-critical-shutdown threshold from 90°F to 80°F, to shut down non-critical load earlier and more conservatively than today's policy allows. This was discussed and not adopted; Infrastructure Operations noted 80°F is within the range temperatures can reach briefly during normal planned maintenance on a single cooling unit, and a lower threshold would cause unnecessary non-critical shutdowns during routine, planned single-unit maintenance windows, creating availability problems for no real safety benefit in return.

ACTIONS ADOPTED
1. Move Cooling Unit 3-B's bearing replacement up from the scheduled February window to this week, given it already failed once (owner: Facilities, due January 27).
2. Review all pods' cooling units with any open vibration-inspection flags and prioritize replacement scheduling accordingly, rather than defaulting to the next routine window (owner: Bram Vandermeer, due February 5).
3. No change to the 90°F non-critical-shutdown threshold, per the discussion above.

SIGN-OFF
Approved by Bram Vandermeer, Infrastructure Operations Lead, January 24.

CASCADIA MUNICIPAL EMPLOYEES PENSION FUND
Investment Committee Meeting Minutes
Date: August 14 | Recorded by: Anouk Verstappen

ATTENDANCE
Present: Committee Chair Wanjiru Kamau, Members Tariq Idris, Consuela Marques, Gideon Farley. Investment Consultant: Piotr Zielinski (Halvorsen Advisory Group).

PERFORMANCE REVIEW
Consultant Zielinski reported the fund returned 4.2% for the quarter, against a blended benchmark return of 3.8%, an outperformance of 0.4 percentage points. Year-to-date, the fund is up 7.1% against a benchmark of 6.9%. Total fund assets stand at $340 million as of quarter-end, up from $326 million at the start of the year.

PROPOSAL 1: REAL ESTATE ALLOCATION
Zielinski presented a proposal to reallocate 5% of the portfolio, approximately $17 million, from the fund's investment-grade bond allocation into a new core-plus real estate investment trust fund, to improve diversification and inflation-hedging characteristics given the fund's long-duration liabilities. After discussion of the REIT fund's fee structure and liquidity terms, quarterly redemption with a 45-day notice period, Tariq Idris moved to approve the 5% reallocation. Consuela Marques seconded. The motion passed 4-0.

PROPOSAL 2: EQUITY ALLOCATION INCREASE
Gideon Farley separately proposed increasing the fund's public equity allocation by 8 percentage points, funded by further reducing the bond allocation, arguing the fund's long time horizon justified more growth-oriented positioning overall. Zielinski cautioned that the fund's actuarial schedule shows a meaningfully larger benefit-payment obligation in years 6 through 9 than previously modeled, following last year's actuarial update, which argues for maintaining more near-term liquidity than an 8-point equity increase would leave available. After discussion, the committee voted 1-3, Farley in favor, against the equity increase. The proposal did not pass; the fund's equity allocation remains unchanged this quarter, aside from whatever secondary effect the approved REIT reallocation has on relative portfolio weightings going forward.

DISCUSSION: COMBINED EFFECT
Kamau asked Zielinski to confirm the REIT reallocation, being funded from bonds rather than equity, does not itself change the fund's equity allocation percentage in any way. Zielinski confirmed: the 5% reallocation moves money from bonds to real estate only; equity allocation is entirely unaffected by Proposal 1 and remains at its current target following today's meeting, since Proposal 2, the equity increase, did not pass at all.

FEE REVIEW
The committee reviewed annual investment management fees, currently 0.62% of assets under management blended across all managers, and asked Zielinski to benchmark this figure against peer pension funds of similar size before the November meeting for comparison, noting fee levels have not been formally benchmarked against peers in over three years.

NEXT STEPS
Zielinski will begin transition into the new REIT fund over the next 60 days, in tranches, to avoid transacting the full $17 million at a single point in time and to reduce market-timing risk. Zielinski will also prepare the peer fee benchmarking analysis requested above for the November meeting.

MANAGER WATCH LIST
Zielinski also gave a brief update on the fund's active manager roster: one small-cap equity manager remains on the watch list established last quarter after underperforming its benchmark for three consecutive quarters, though performance improved this quarter and the committee agreed to review again in November before making any change. No managers were added to or removed from the roster at this meeting.

MEMBER COMMUNICATIONS
Consuela Marques asked whether this quarter's results and the REIT reallocation should be summarized for plan members in the next newsletter. The committee agreed a brief, plain-language summary would be useful, and asked Zielinski's firm to draft a paragraph for staff review before the newsletter's next publication date.

ADJOURNMENT
Meeting adjourned at 4:35 p.m. Next meeting: November 13.

Minutes respectfully submitted by Anouk Verstappen, Committee Recording Secretary.
